questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical governance of resources in a namespace, a common production constraint. It also probes how candidates apply quota and limit controls to real workloads.

## Key Concepts
- ResourceQuota and LimitRange interplay
- requests vs limits, scheduling behavior, and event inspection
- Rollback strategies and observability

## Code Example
```yaml
# ResourceQuota
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: rq-ops
  namespace: ops
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "40"
    requests.memory: "160Gi"
    limits.cpu: "80"
    limits.memory: "320Gi"
```
```yaml
# LimitRange
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: lr-ops
  namespace: ops
spec:
  limits:
  - defaultRequest:
      cpu: 100m
      memory: 128Mi
    defaultLimit:
      cpu: 300m
      memory: 512Mi
    max:
      cpu: "2"
      memory: 1Gi
    type: Container
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to design a per-namespace config pipeline that validates and applies manifests safely inside the cluster while coordinating with a central portal. It exercises InitContainers, in-cluster validation, ConfigMaps/Secrets usage, and network isolation.

## Key Concepts
- Per-namespace resource provisioning from a PVC
- InitContainer tooling bootstrap (kubectl, yq)
- In-cluster manifest validation via kubectl dry-run
- Runtime config with ConfigMap (BATCH_SIZE)
- Secrets for external portals and TLS cert rotation
- Namespace NetworkPolicy for egress control

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: config-sync
data:
  BATCH_SIZE: "50"
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: config-syncer
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    spec:
      initContainers:
        - name: install-tools
          image: alpine:3.18
          command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache curl kubectl yq"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: config
              mountPath: /config
      containers:
        - name: watcher
          image: alpine:3.18
          command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "while true; do sleep 30; done"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: config
              mountPath: /config
      volumes:
        - name: config
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: config-pvc
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test failure modes if a manifest is invalid after initial processing?
- What changes would you make to scale this for many namespaces?

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: heartbeat-runner
  namespace: target-ns
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: heartbeat-runner
```

## Why This Is Asked

Assesses ability to choreograph ephemeral canaries using core CKAD primitives: templated Deployment from ConfigMap, secret-based auth, logs via PVC, init containers, probes, and namespace-scoped NetworkPolicy.

## Key Concepts

- ConfigMap templating for Deployment
- Secret-based API tokens and restricted RBAC
- PVC-backed logs and cleanup discipline
- InitContainers for tooling bootstrap
- Readiness/Liveness probes for short-lived canaries
- NetworkPolicy scoped to external dashboard

## Code Example

```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: canary-tester
spec:
  schedule: "*/20 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          initContainers:
            - name: install-tools
              image: alpine:3.18
              command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache curl jq"]
          containers:
            - name: canary
              image: my-canary-image:latest
              command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "/canary/run.sh"]
              env:
                - name: DASHBOARD_TOKEN
                  valueFrom:
                    secretKeyRef:
                      name: canary-token
                      key: token
              volumeMounts:
                - name: logs
                  mountPath: /logs
          volumes:
            - name: logs
              persistentVolumeClaim:
                claimName: canary-logs
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you rollback a failing canary and propagate the status to the dashboard?
- What are the memory/CPU considerations for rapid-canary spikes and how would you cap them?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests CKAD ability to combine common primitives: PVC-backed data, ConfigMap-driven behavior, Secrets for credentials, InitContainers, TLS rotation sidecar, probes, and per-namespace NetworkPolicy in a cohesive, beginner-friendly scenario.

## Key Concepts
- ConfigMap/Secret usage for runtime config and credentials
- PVC-backed storage and data lifecycle
- InitContainer for dependencies
- TLS cert rotation sidecar
- Readiness/Liveness probes and health checks
- NamespaceNetworkPolicy scoping

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: ns-api
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: ns-api
    spec:
      volumes:
        - name: data
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: ns-app-data
      initContainers:
        - name: install-deps
          image: python:3.11
          command: ["bash","-lc","pip install flask sqlite3"]
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: myregistry/ns-api:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          env:
            - name: ENABLE_FEATURE
              valueFrom:
                configMapKeyRef:
                  name: app-config
                  key: ENABLE_FEATURE
            - name: API_TIMEOUT
              valueFrom:
                configMapKeyRef:
                  name: app-config
                  key: API_TIMEOUT
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /data
      - name: tls-sidecar
        image: quay.io/cert_manager/tls-sidecar:latest
        # sidecar config omitted for brevity
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
      restartPolicy: Always
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test config flag changes without rolling pods?
- What are trade-offs of storing DB in a PVC vs ephemeral storage?

## Why This Is Asked
Explores per-namespace data ingestion, config-driven parsing, and strict egress controls—core CKAD topics with practical trade-offs.

## Key Concepts
- ConfigMaps for runtime parsing rules
- PVC-backed logs and InitContainers for tooling
- Secrets for credentials and tokens
- TLS sidecar and cert rotation
- Readiness/Liveness probes
- Namespace NetworkPolicy egress controls

## Code Example
```yaml
# Minimal skeleton: Deployment, PVC, ConfigMap/Secret refs
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: log-router
  namespace: <namespace>
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: log-router
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: log-router
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: install-tools
        image: alpine:3.18
        command: ["/bin/sh","-c","apk add --no-cache awk sed curl"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
      containers:
      - name: router
        image: myorg/log-router:latest
        env:
        - name: REGEX
          valueFrom:
            configMapKeyRef:
              name: log-config
              key: regex
        - name: BATCH_SIZE
          valueFrom:
            configMapKeyRef:
              name: log-config
              key: batchSize
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
      volumes:
      - name: logs
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: logs-pvc
      - name: tls
        secret:
          secretName: log-tls
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test the regex parsing and batching in a SRP-safe way?
- What metrics would you expose for reliability and observability?

## Why This Is Asked
CKAD candidates often struggle with end-to-end file ingestion using Kubernetes primitives. This question tests volume access, ConfigMap/Secret usage, InitContainers, probes, NetworkPolicy, and retry strategies in a comprehensive scenario.

## Key Concepts
- ConfigMaps/Secrets for configuration and credentials
- InitContainers for tooling setup
- In-cluster networking and security policies
- File-based ingestion with idempotent POST operations
- Multi-container pod patterns

## Code Example
```javascript
// Pseudo-implementation sketch
const payload = readFile('/input/file.json');
validateSchema(payload, getSchema('schema-config'));
const normalized = normalize(payload);
sendToEndpoint('http://data-portal:8080/api/v1/ingest', normalized);
```

## Trade-offs
- **File watching vs. event-driven**: File watching is simpler but less efficient than event-based systems
- **In-cluster validation**: Validates locally but increases pod resource usage
- **NetworkPolicy restrictions**: Improves security but adds complexity to egress management
- **Sidecar overhead**: TLS rotation adds reliability but increases resource consumption

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question evaluates comprehensive Kubernetes application design skills including file-driven data processing, runtime tool provisioning, batch processing workflows, secure external communications, and network security isolation patterns commonly required in enterprise environments.

## Key Concepts
- **InitContainer tool provisioning**: Installing tar and jq utilities for runtime data processing
- **PVC data ingestion**: Processing Docker tarball files from persistent storage
- **ConfigMap-driven configuration**: Dynamic batching parameter (BATCH_SIZE) management
- **Secret-based authentication**: Secure API token handling for external communications
- **TLS certificate lifecycle management**: Sidecar pattern for certificate rotation
- **Container health monitoring**: Readiness and liveness probe implementation
- **Network security**: Namespace NetworkPolicy for egress traffic restriction

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: image-audit
  namespace: target-namespace
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: install-tools
        image: alpine:latest
        command: ['sh', '-c', 'apk add --no-cache tar jq']
        volumeMounts:
        - name: bin
          mountPath: /usr/local/bin
      containers:
      - name: audit-processor
        image: audit-service:latest
        env:
        - name: BATCH_SIZE
          valueFrom:
            configMapKeyRef:
              name: audit-config
              key: BATCH_SIZE
        - name: API_TOKEN
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: audit-secret
              key: token
        volumeMounts:
        - name: images
          mountPath: /images
        - name: bin
          mountPath: /usr/local/bin
      - name: cert-rotator
```

## Why This Is Asked

## Code Example
```yaml
# Deployment skeleton (aggregator)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: aggregator
  namespace: analytics
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        checksum/config: <CONFIGMAP_SHA>
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: aggregator
        image: your-image
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        volumeMounts:
        - name: data-input
          mountPath: /data/input
        - name: data-output
          mountPath: /data/output
        - name: config
          mountPath: /etc/aggregator
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "100m"
            memory: "128Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "512Mi"
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /readyz
            port: 8080
        startupProbe:
          tcpSocket:
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 20
          periodSeconds: 5
          timeoutSeconds: 2
          failureThreshold: 12
        lifecycle:
          preStop:
            exec:
              command: ["/bin/sleep", "5"]
      volumes:
      - name: data-input
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: input-pvc
      - name: data-output
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: output-pvc
      - name: config
        configMap:
          name: aggregator-conf
---
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: aggregator-pdb
  namespace: analytics
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: aggregator
```

## Why This Is Asked
This question tests practical CKAD skills, including permissioning, automation, and Kubernetes-native policy enforcement using a CronJob with ConfigMap-driven behavior.

## Key Concepts
- Namespace-scoped CronJob for periodic enforcement
- ConfigMap-driven policy configuration (imageRepo, imageTag)
- kubectl patch or server-side apply for image updates
- PVC-based logging and HTTP POST for audit trails
- InitContainer for tooling installation (curl, jq)
- Namespace NetworkPolicy scoping for egress control

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: image-tag-enforcer
  namespace: default
spec:
  schedule: "*/5 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          initContainers:
          - name: installer
            image: busybox
            command: ["sh", "-c", "apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl jq"]
          containers:
          - name: enforcer
            image: curlimages/curl:latest
            command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
            args:
            - |
              # Read policy from ConfigMap
              # Get all Deployments in namespace
              # Compare images against policy
              # Patch mismatched Deployments
              # Write heartbeat log to /logs
              # POST summary to policy-portal
            volumeMounts:
            - name: log-volume
              mountPath: /logs
            readinessProbe:
              exec:
                command: ["test", "-f", "/logs/ready"]
              initialDelaySeconds: 5
              periodSeconds: 10
            livenessProbe:
              exec:
                command: ["test", "-f", "/logs/alive"]
              initialDelaySeconds: 15
              periodSeconds: 20
          volumes:
          - name: log-volume
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: enforcer-logs
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: restrict-egress
  namespace: default
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: policy-portal
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 8080
```

## Trade-offs
- **Frequency**: Running every 5 minutes balances responsiveness vs. resource usage; longer intervals reduce API load but delay remediation
- **PVC vs. Sidecar**: Using a PVC is simpler but requires storage provisioning; a sidecar could stream logs directly
- **Patch vs. Reconcile Controller**: A declarative controller would be more robust but requires custom operator development; CronJob is quicker to implement but imperative
- **InitContainer**: Pre-installing tools increases pod startup time; consider using a custom image with tools baked in instead
- **NetworkPolicy**: Restricting egress improves security but may break legitimate communication; ensure all required endpoints are explicitly allowed
- **Idempotency**: Multiple enforcers running simultaneously could cause conflicts; consider adding a lock mechanism or using `concurrencyPolicy: Forbid`

## Why This Is Asked

- Readiness/Liveness probes for the Job Pod

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: canary-upgrade
spec:
  schedule: "*/10 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          serviceAccountName: canary-sa
          initContainers:
          - name: install-tools
            image: alpine:3.17
            command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache curl jq; true"]
            volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
          containers:
          - name: upgrader
            image: bitnami/kubectl:latest
            command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "set -e; CANARY_TAG=$(kubectl get configmap canary-config -o jsonpath='{.data.tag}'); kubectl patch deployment my-app -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"my-app","image":"myrepo/my-app:${CANARY_TAG}"}]}}}}' --record; echo done; sleep 1"]
            volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
          volumes:
          - name: logs
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: logs-pvc
          imagePullSecrets:
          - name: registry-credentials
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
```

## Why This Is Asked

Tests practical CKAD debugging: handling slow-start upgrades with probes, init containers for bootstrapping state, and PD&B safeguards to prevent downtime during maintenance.

## Key Concepts

- startupProbe and readinessProbe tuning
- initContainer for pre-warming caches
- PodDisruptionBudget for upgrade safety
- RollingUpdate strategy and rollback procedures

## Code Example

```yaml
# Minimal patch sketch (Deployment snippet)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: invoice-processor
  namespace: payments
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: init-cache
        image: invoice-processor:2.1
        command: ["sh", "-c", "cp /config/* /var/cache/ || true"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: config
          mountPath: /config
        - name: cache
          mountPath: /var/cache
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: invoice-processor:2.1
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 30
          periodSeconds: 10
      volumes:
      - name: config
        secret:
          secretName: app-secret
      - name: cache
        emptyDir: {}
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you adapt this for a cluster with limited CPU headroom?
- What metrics would you monitor to confirm startup health and cache warmth?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Tests ability to design a namespace-scoped TLS gateway leveraging CRD, InitContainer, Secrets, and a ready path tied to certificate availability.

## Key Concepts

- CustomResourceDefinition for per-namespace gateways
- InitContainer fetching TLS certs via Vault-like API
- Secrets mounted into gateway for TLS material
- Readiness/Liveness linked to cert presence/expiry; logs to a PVC

## Code Example

```yaml
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: tlsgateways.example.com
spec:
  group: example.com
  versions:
  - name: v1
    served: true
    storage: true
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          spec:
            type: object
            properties:
              serviceName:
                type: string
              port:
                type: integer
              hostname:
                type: string
              apiTokenSecret:
                type: string
```

```yaml
apiVersion: example.com/v1
kind: TLSGateway
metadata:
  name: my-service-gateway
  namespace: default
spec:
  serviceName: my-service
  port: 443
  hostname: app.example.com
  apiTokenSecret: tlsgateway-token
```

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: tls-gateway
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: tls-gateway
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: tls-gateway
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: fetch-certs
        image: curlimages/curl:8.1
        command: ["sh", "-c", "curl -sS http://vault.example/api/cert -o /certs/tls.crt"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: certs
          mountPath: /certs
      containers:
      - name: envoy
        image: envoyproxy/envoy:v1.23.0
        ports:
        - containerPort: 443
        volumeMounts:
        - name: certs
          mountPath: /etc/envoy/certs
      volumes:
      - name: certs
        secret:
          secretName: tlsgateway-certs
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you handle cert rotation cadence and revocation?
- What RBAC would you implement for the InitContainer to access the API token?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Tests CRD API access from a pod, ConfigMap-driven runtime configuration, Secret-based credentials, InitContainer usage, and proper observability with probes and PVC-backed logs. It also touches network isolation via NetworkPolicy in a CKAD-appropriate setting.

## Key Concepts

- CRD watch and API access from a namespace-scoped Pod
- ConfigMap as dynamic WINDOW configuration
- Secret-stored Bearer token for outbound POST
- InitContainer for tooling installation
- Readiness/Liveness probes for a long-running auditor
- Logs persisted to a PVC
- Namespace NetworkPolicy restricting egress

## Code Example

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
data:
  audit-config: |
    window: 60
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
data:
  audit-token: <base64-encoded-token>
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: crd-auditor
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: crd-auditor
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: crd-auditor
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: crd-auditor-sa
      initContainers:
      - name: install-tools
        image: alpine:3.18
        command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache curl jq"]
        volumeMounts:
        - mountPath: /logs
          name: logs
      containers:
      - name: auditor
        image: my-registry/crd-auditor:latest
        env:
        - name: AUDIT_CONFIG
          valueFrom:
            configMapKeyRef:
              name: audit-config
              key: window
        - name: AUDIT_TOKEN
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: audit-token
              key: token
        volumeMounts:
        - mountPath: /logs
          name: logs
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
      volumes:
      - name: logs
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: crd-auditor-logs
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you simulate CRD changes locally for tests?
- How would you handle CRD API version upgrades and backward compatibility?
